newsitem.title: USA: WHEAT -- Karnal bunt a headache for U.S. exporters.
newsitem.headline: WHEAT -- Karnal bunt a headache for U.S. exporters.

text.p: Karnal bunt fungus spreads easily and is hard to treat, and while it causes no known health problems in consumers it is proving a major headache for U.S. exporters and regulators, plant pathologists said.
"This fungus is very efficient and finds its way wherever wheat goes and is grown," said R. James Cook, U.S. Agriculture Department plant pathologist in Washington state.
"I think that as seed is moved, we will find the fungus in the shipping channels more and more," Cook said. "I think it's a given that we will find it."
Karnal bunt, a fungal disease that can lower yields and causes a harmless but unpleasant odor and taste, was detected in U.S. wheat for the first time on record in March, 1996.

That discovery, in durum wheat seed grown in Arizona, led to a quarantine by government authorities and a temporary freeze to U.S. wheat exports, since a condition for most purchases demands fungus-free certification by foreign buyers.
Karnal bunt was later found in wheat in California, New Mexico, Texas, Alabama and, just last week, Tennessee.
"We don't know where karnal bunt will develop," Cook said, adding that more research is needed.
That presents a major problem for sellers of U.S. wheat, since buyers often now specify that the wheat purchased must orginate from an area with no known exposure to karnal bunt.
Several major importers, including China, have refused to accept wheat containing the fungus.

But because the fungus is easy to transport and hard to detect, it may already exist in major U.S. wheat growing areas. U.S. exporters may not be able to guarantee the wheat came from bunt-free areas.
"If you don't find the fungus in the area that you looked, it doesn't mean it hasn't been through there," Cook said.
The fungus, named for a region in India where it was first discovered, likely spread into the United States from Mexico, where it was detected in 1970.

It grows best in climates similar to India with warm, dry weather during fallow periods and cool, moist soil conditions during flowering, said Merritt Nelson, professor of plant pathology at the University of Arizona.
"It does not appear to occur in areas that have very cold winters," he said. "The spores can survive up to five years in the soil but it depends on how much moisture is in the soil."
While it was first found in durum wheat grown in Arizona, other varieties of wheat are more susceptible. Last week in Tennessee, it was found in soft red winter wheat.

USDA established a quarantine in Arizona to try to contain the fungus, but treating it is difficult, said Larry Butler, a product development manager at Wilbur-Ellis, an agricultural chemical firm based in Liberty, Missouri.

"Their biology is very dissimilar to other bunts and smuts," Butler said. "You have to have some treatment that will kill the spore or something that will kill the invading fungus at the time of infection (flowering)."
Butler, who studied karnal bunt while working with the Mexico-based International Maize and Wheat Improvement Center, said it is resistant to many fungicides.
"A lot of these (fungicides) will have some success in reducing it, but you will not eliminate it," Butler said.
Farmers can take precautions to slow the spread, he added.
If karnal bunt has been detected in the area, they must make sure there are no spores in the soil before they plant.
"The seed that (the farmer) would plant would have to be certified free of karnal bunt and he would have to use some sort of seed treatment," Butler said.
But the fungus is also spread by air, farm machinery and transport equipment, University of Arizona's Nelson said.
"The spores are very light and do blow by the wind," he said. The fungus "is also spread in boxcars, trucks, any conveyances that have had infected wheat in them."
USDA established a testing program and samples have been taken from many wheat-growing areas across the country but Cook said the spores may exist undetected in small amounts.
"We're finding it in the South so far because it's been handy to come in from Mexico," Cook said.
In order to search the rest of the country as thoroughly, scientists estimated USDA would need to test three million to our million wheat fields, he said. (Chicago Newsdesk 312-408-8749)
